questions.question: The Whole Circle Bearing (WCB) of line AB is 150°. The length of AB is 100 m. The latitude and departure values, respectively, for this line are:
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Compass Surveying & Traversing

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Length of line \(AB\): \(L = 100\) m
    • Whole Circle Bearing: \(\theta = 150^\circ\)
  • Aim: Calculate Latitude (\(Lat\)) and Departure (\(Dep\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Latitude: Projection on N-S axis = \(L \cos\theta\)
  • Departure: Projection on E-W axis = \(L \sin\theta\)
  • Sign Convention: North/East = \((+)\); South/West = \((-)\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Latitude:
    \[Lat = 100 \times \cos(150^\circ) = 100 \times (-\cos 30^\circ) = 100 \times (-0.8660) = -86.60 \text{ m}\]
  2. Departure:
    \[Dep = 100 \times \sin(150^\circ) = 100 \times \sin(30^\circ) = 100 \times 0.5000 = +50.00 \text{ m}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(Lat = -86.60\) m; \(Dep = +50.00\) m  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
A 30 m long tape is standardized at 25 °C. It was used to measure the length of a line which came out to be 200 m. The temperature during the measurement was 35 °C. The coefficient of expansion of the tape was \( 11 \times 10^{-6} \) per °C. The correction in the measured length (in mm) due to change in temperature is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Temperature Correction)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Nominal tape length = 30 m
    • Standardization temperature: \(T_0 = 25^\circ\)C
    • Measured length: \(L = 200\) m
    • Measurement temperature: \(T_m = 35^\circ\)C
    • Coefficient of expansion: \(\alpha = 11 \times 10^{-6}\) /°C
  • Aim: Find total temperature correction in mm.

3. Core Concepts:

When \(T_m > T_0\), the tape expands and reads short → positive correction applied:

\[C_t = \alpha \cdot (T_m - T_0) \cdot L\]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Apply formula:
    \[C_t = (11 \times 10^{-6}) \times (35 - 25) \times 200\]
    \[C_t = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 2000 = 22 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}\]
  2. Convert to mm:
    \[C_t = 22 \text{ mm}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: +22 mm  |  Accepted key range: 22 to 22

The height of the plane of collimation of a levelling instrument is 100.000 m from a datum. The levelling instrument measures a Back Sight of 1.500 m on a vertically held staff at a ground point P. The reduced level (in m) of the ground point P with respect to the datum is _______
(rounded off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Height of Instrument (HI) = 100.000 m
    • Back Sight (BS) staff reading at point P = 1.500 m
  • Aim: Determine the Reduced Level (RL) of point P in m.

3. Core Concepts:

The Height of Instrument (HI) is the absolute elevation of the line of sight. The staff reading is the vertical distance from the ground point up to the line of sight:

\[RL = HI - \text{Staff Reading}\]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \[RL_P = 100.000 - 1.500 = 98.500 \text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 98.500 m  |  Accepted key range: 98.500 to 98.500

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q43

questions.question: Locations \( P \) and \( Q \) are separated by a wide valley. The difference in levels of locations \( P \) and \( Q \) measured by a levelling instrument stationed near \( P \) is 3.0 m. The same instrument stationed near \( Q \) measures the difference in levels of locations \( P \) and \( Q \) as -1.0 m. Assume that the atmospheric refraction is same during the measurements. The true difference in levels (in m) of locations \( P \) and \( Q \) is
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Apparent difference in elevation from instrument at \(P\): \(\Delta h_1 = +3.0\) m
    • Apparent difference in elevation from instrument at \(Q\): \(\Delta h_2 = -1.0\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the true difference in levels between locations \(P\) and \(Q\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Reciprocal Levelling: Used when the instrument cannot be set up midway (e.g., across a wide valley). Observations from both banks eliminate errors due to Earth's curvature, atmospheric refraction, and collimation error.
  • Formula:
    \[\Delta H = \dfrac{\Delta h_1 + \Delta h_2}{2}\]
    (Sign convention: elevation difference = \(E_Q - E_P\))

4. Solution Method & Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the equation:
    Let \(\Delta H\) = true elevation difference (\(\text{Level}_Q - \text{Level}_P\)).
    \(\Delta h_1 = +3.0\) m, \(\Delta h_2 = -1.0\) m.
  2. Calculate True Difference:
    \[\Delta H = \dfrac{3.0 + (-1.0)}{2} = \dfrac{2.0}{2} = 1.0 \text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Calculated result: 1.0 m  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.question:
The following consecutive readings (in m) were taken with a dumpy level and a levelling staff at a common interval of 20 m:
0.385; 1.030; 1.925; 2.825; 3.730; 4.850; 1.045; 2.005; 3.330; 4.580

The dumpy level was shifted after taking the sixth reading.

The gradient (in %) of the ground between the first and the last location of the reading is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • 10 consecutive staff readings (m): 0.385, 1.030, 1.925, 2.825, 3.730, 4.850, 1.045, 2.005, 3.330, 4.580
    • Interval = 20 m; Instrument shifted after the 6th reading.
  • Aim: Calculate the ground gradient (%) between the first and last staff location.

3. Core Concepts:

  • First reading of each setup = Back Sight (BS); last reading before shifting = Fore Sight (FS); others = Intermediate Sights (IS).
  • Total Elevation Difference: \(\Delta H = \sum BS - \sum FS\)
  • Gradient (%): \(\left(\dfrac{\Delta H}{\text{Total Distance}}\right) \times 100\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Categorize readings:
    SetupReading No.TypeValue (m)
    Setup 11BS0.385
    2IS1.030
    3IS1.925
    4IS2.825
    5IS3.730
    6FS4.850
    Setup 27BS1.045
    8IS2.005
    9IS3.330
    10FS4.580
  2. Total Elevation Difference:
    \[\sum BS = 0.385 + 1.045 = 1.430 \text{ m}\]
    \[\sum FS = 4.850 + 4.580 = 9.430 \text{ m}\]
    \[\Delta H = 1.430 - 9.430 = -8.000 \text{ m}\]
    (Negative: last station is 8 m lower than first.)
  3. Horizontal Distance:
    Readings 6 and 7 are at the same station → total stations = 9 → intervals = 8.
    \(L = 8 \times 20 = 160\) m.
  4. Gradient:
    \[\text{Gradient} = \dfrac{-8.000}{160} \times 100 = -5\%\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: −5% (falling gradient of 5%)  |  Accepted key range: −5 to −5 (or 5 to 5)

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE with respect to levelling survey?
options: A level surface at all points is normal to the direction of the force of gravity.
Two level surfaces can cross each other.
Ellipsoid is an irregular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.
Geoid is a regular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: A level surface at all points is normal to the direction of the force of gravity.
structuredOptions.html: A level surface at all points is normal to the direction of the force of gravity.

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: Two level surfaces can cross each other.
structuredOptions.html: Two level surfaces can cross each other.

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: Ellipsoid is an irregular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.
structuredOptions.html: Ellipsoid is an irregular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Geoid is a regular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.
structuredOptions.html: Geoid is a regular surface approximating the physical surface of the Earth.

questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four statements relating to surfaces in levelling.
  • Aim: Identify the TRUE statement among the choices.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Level Surface: An equipotential surface of the Earth's gravity field. A plumb line (direction of gravity) is perpendicular (normal) to a level surface at all points.
  • Intersection: Two equipotential surfaces (level surfaces) possessing different potentials can never cross each other.
  • Geoid vs. Ellipsoid: The Geoid is an equipotential surface at Mean Sea Level (irregular shape). The Ellipsoid is a purely mathematical, regular geometry approximating the earth.

Analyze each option fundamentally:

  • (B) Two level surfaces can cross each other. → FALSE
  • (C) Ellipsoid is an irregular surface. → FALSE (it is regular mathematical geometry)
  • (D) Geoid is a regular surface. → FALSE (it is an irregular equipotential surface)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

The definition of a level surface verifies that its fundamental characteristic is being normal (at \(90^\circ\)) to the direction of gravity force everywhere.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: A level surface at all points is normal to the direction of the force of gravity. | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q35

questions.question: A tourist visiting a city holds a map prepared at a scale of 1:25000. The tourist measures the distance between place A and place B in the city as 12.0 cm on the map. Assuming both the places are connected by a straight road, the distance (in km) the tourist needs to walk from A to B is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Scale and Distance

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Representative Fraction Map Scale \(= 1 : 25{,}000\)
    • Distance on map \(= 12.0\text{ cm}\)
  • Aim: Convert the map distance to actual ground distance in km.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Scale relation: \(\text{Ground Distance} = \text{Map Distance} \times \text{Scale Factor}\)
  • Unit conversions: \(100\text{ cm} = 1\text{ m}\) and \(1000\text{ m} = 1\text{ km}\)  \(\Rightarrow 1\text{ km} = 10^5\text{ cm}\)

4. Solution Method:

Multiply the map distance by the scale denominator to get the ground distance in cm, then convert to km.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Ground distance in cm:\[\text{Distance}_{\text{ground}} = 12.0\text{ cm} \times 25{,}000 = 3{,}00{,}000\text{ cm} \]
  2. Convert to kilometers:\[\text{Distance}_{\text{ground (km)}} = \dfrac{3{,}00{,}000}{1{,}00{,}000} = 3\text{ km} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3 km | Accepted key range: 3 to 3

  • Fore Sight (FS): The last staff reading taken before moving the instrument (on a point to be determined or change point).

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
Interior angles measured at the locations of a closed traverse ABCDA are given in table below.

LocationInterior angle
A71° 1' 40''
B104° 54' 23''
C107° 54' 10''
D76° 20' 42''

The total error in the measured angles (in degrees) is _____________ (rounded off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Traverse)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Interior angles of 4-sided closed traverse ABCDA:
    • \(A = 71^\circ 1' 40''\)
    • \(B = 104^\circ 54' 23''\)
    • \(C = 107^\circ 54' 10''\)
    • \(D = 76^\circ 20' 42''\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total angular error in decimal degrees (rounded to 3 decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Theoretical sum for \(n\)-sided polygon: \(\Sigma_{\text{theoretical}} = (2n-4) \times 90^\circ\)
  • Angular Error: \(\text{Error} = \Sigma_{\text{measured}} - \Sigma_{\text{theoretical}}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Sum the measured angles in DMS.
  2. Calculate the theoretical sum for \(n = 4\).
  3. Find the DMS error and convert to decimal degrees.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Sum of Seconds: \(40 + 23 + 10 + 42 = 115'' = 1' + 55''\)  (carry \(1'\))
  2. Sum of Minutes: \(1 + 54 + 54 + 20 + 1_{\text{carry}} = 130' = 2^\circ + 10'\)  (carry \(2^\circ\))
  3. Sum of Degrees: \(71 + 104 + 107 + 76 + 2_{\text{carry}} = 360^\circ\)
  4. Total Measured Sum: \(360^\circ 10' 55''\)
  5. Theoretical Sum (\(n=4\)):\[\Sigma_{\text{theoretical}} = (2 \times 4 - 4) \times 90^\circ = 360^\circ \]
  6. Angular Error:\[\text{Error} = 360^\circ 10' 55'' - 360^\circ 0' 0'' = 0^\circ 10' 55'' \]
  7. Convert to Decimal Degrees:\[\text{Error} = 0 + \dfrac{10}{60} + \dfrac{55}{3600} = 0.16667 + 0.01528 = 0.18194^\circ \approx 0.182^\circ \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.182° | Accepted key range: 0.180 to 0.184

questions.question: If the horizontal distance between a staff point and the point of observation is \( d \), the error due to the curvature of earth is proportional to
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Levelling / Earth's Curvature Error

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Horizontal distance \(d\).
  • Aim: Determine what the error due to earth's curvature is proportional to.

Core Concepts:

Curvature Correction (\(C_c\)): A level line is a curved line parallel to the earth's surface, but the line of sight is horizontal (tangent). The vertical departure between the horizontal line and the level line is the curvature error.

\[C_c = \dfrac{d^2}{2R} \]

where \(d\) is horizontal distance and \(R\) is the radius of the earth.

Solution:

  1. State the formula: Error \(= \dfrac{d^2}{2R}\).
  2. Since \(2R\) (diameter of the earth) is a constant, the error is directly proportional to \(d^2\).

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Proportional to \(d^2\) | Option: C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q27
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: If the quadrantal bearing of a line is N30°W, then the whole circle bearing of the line is
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Bearings (Quadrantal to Whole Circle Bearing)

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Quadrantal Bearing (QB) of line: \(\text{N}30^\circ\text{W}\) (angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\))
  • Aim: Convert the given quadrantal bearing to whole circle bearing (WCB).

Core Concepts

Theory: A quadrantal bearing is measured from the nearer North/South meridian toward East/West, limited to \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\). A whole circle bearing is measured clockwise from North, ranging \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\).

Formulas (QB \(\to\) WCB):
Let \(\theta\) be the acute angle in the quadrantal bearing.

  • NE quadrant (N\(\theta\)E): \(\text{WCB} = \theta\)
  • SE quadrant (S\(\theta\)E): \(\text{WCB} = 180^\circ - \theta\)
  • SW quadrant (S\(\theta\)W): \(\text{WCB} = 180^\circ + \theta\)
  • NW quadrant (N\(\theta\)W): \(\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - \theta\)

Standard assumptions: Bearings are referenced to North; WCB is measured clockwise.

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: Identify the quadrant from the QB notation (N/S first, then E/W) \(\rightarrow\) choose the corresponding conversion formula \(\rightarrow\) compute WCB.
  • Alternative: Visualize the azimuth clockwise from North; for N\(\theta\)W, rotate \(\theta\) anticlockwise from North, hence clockwise bearing is \(360^\circ-\theta\).
  • Common pitfalls to avoid: (i) Using \(180^\circ \pm \theta\) for NW cases, (ii) forgetting that WCB is clockwise from North.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Identify quadrant: \(\text{N}30^\circ\text{W}\) lies in the NW quadrant (from North towards West) with \(\theta = 30^\circ\).
  2. Apply NW conversion:
    \[\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - \theta \]
  3. Substitute and compute:
    \[\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ \]

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: NW bearings must yield WCB between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\). The computed \(330^\circ\) satisfies this, so the result is physically consistent.

Final Answer

Final Answer: \(330^\circ\) | Option(s): D

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
In levelling between two points A and B on the opposite banks of a river, the readings are taken by setting the instrument both at A and B, as shown in the table. If the RL of A is 150.000 m, the RL of B (in m) is _______________ (rounded off to 3 decimal places).

Level positionStaff readings
AB
A1.8001.350
B1.4500.950
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying / Reciprocal Levelling

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Instrument at A: Staff reading on A (\(a_1\)) = 1.800 m, Staff reading on B (\(b_1\)) = 1.350 m
    Instrument at B: Staff reading on A (\(a_2\)) = 1.450 m, Staff reading on B (\(b_2\)) = 0.950 m
    RL of A = 150.000 m
  • Aim: Calculate RL of B in meters, rounded to 3 decimal places.

Core Concepts:

Reciprocal Levelling: Eliminates errors due to Earth's curvature, atmospheric refraction, and instrument collimation by averaging two observations from opposite ends.

True Difference in Elevation:

\[h = \dfrac{(a_1 - b_1) + (a_2 - b_2)}{2} \]

Sign Convention: If staff reading at A > reading at B, point B is physically higher.

Solution:

  1. Apparent difference from instrument at A:
    \[\Delta h_1 = a_1 - b_1 = 1.800 - 1.350 = 0.450 \text{ m} \quad (\text{B appears higher}) \]
  2. Apparent difference from instrument at B:
    \[\Delta h_2 = a_2 - b_2 = 1.450 - 0.950 = 0.500 \text{ m} \quad (\text{B appears higher}) \]
  3. True difference in elevation:
    \[h = \dfrac{0.450 + 0.500}{2} = \dfrac{0.950}{2} = 0.475 \text{ m} \]
  4. RL of B:
    \[\text{RL of B} = 150.000 + 0.475 = 150.475 \text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 150.475 m

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
A surveyor measured the distance between two points on the plan drawn to a scale of 1 cm = 40 m and the result was 468 m. Later, it was discovered that the scale used was 1 cm = 20 m.
The true distance between the points (in m) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Map Scales and Measurements

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Computed distance using incorrect scale \(= 468~m\); scale used by surveyor \(= 1~cm : 20~m\); true plan scale \(= 1~cm : 40~m\).
  • Aim: True ground distance, rounded to nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

Ground distance \(=\) plan length (cm) \(\times\) scale factor (m/cm). An error in the scale factor used directly scales the computed distance.

The correct approach is to first recover the true plan length from the wrongly-scaled computation, then apply the correct scale factor.

Common pitfall: Interchanging the "drawn to" and "used" scales.

Solution:

  1. Recover the plan length using the wrong scale:
    \[L_{\text{plan}} \times 20~m/cm = 468~m \Rightarrow L_{\text{plan}} = \dfrac{468}{20} = 23.4~cm\]
  2. Apply the true scale to find the correct ground distance:
    \[\text{True distance} = 23.4~cm \times 40~m/cm = 936~m\]

Final Answer:

936 m

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: If the Fore Bearing of the lines AB and BC are 60° and 122°, respectively, then the interior angle ∠ABC (in degrees) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Compass Surveying

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Fore Bearing (FB) of AB \(= 60^{\circ}\), Fore Bearing of BC \(= 122^{\circ}\).
  • Aim: Determine the interior angle \(\angle ABC\) in degrees.

Core Concepts:

The interior angle at a station in a traverse is the angle enclosed between the preceding line and the forward line.

Back Bearing (BB) \(= \text{FB} + 180^{\circ}\) (if FB \(< 180^{\circ}\)).

Interior Angle \(= \text{BB of preceding line} - \text{FB of forward line}\).

Solution:

  1. Calculate the Back Bearing of line AB:
    \[\text{BB}_{AB} = 60^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 240^{\circ}\]
  2. The angle from line BA (looking back) to line BC (looking forward) is the interior angle \(\angle ABC\).
  3. Calculate Interior Angle:
    \[\angle ABC = 240^{\circ} - 122^{\circ} = 118^{\circ}\]

Final Answer:

118

questions.question: A surveyor observes a zenith angle of 93° 00' 00" during a theodolite survey. The corresponding vertical angle is
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Theodolite (Angle Measurement)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Observed zenith angle = 93° 00' 00"
  • Aim: Determine the corresponding vertical angle.

Core Concepts:

  • Zenith angle is measured from the zenith (vertical upward direction).
  • Vertical angle is measured from the horizontal plane:
    • Zenith angle \(< 90°\) → elevation (positive vertical angle)
    • Zenith angle \(> 90°\) → depression (negative vertical angle)
  • \(\text{Vertical angle} = 90° - \text{Zenith angle}\) (with sign)

Common Pitfall: Confusing zenith angle and vertical angle reference planes.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Zenith angle = 93° 00' 00"
  2. Deviation from horizontal:\[93° - 90° = 3°\text{ below horizontal}\]
  3. Hence vertical angle = −3° 00' 00" (angle of depression).

Final Answer:

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A map is prepared with a scale of 1:1000 and a contour interval of 1 m. If the distance between two adjacent contours on the map is 10 mm, the slope of the ground between the adjacent contours is
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Contouring

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Map Scale = 1:1000
    • Contour Interval (CI) = 1 m
    • Distance between adjacent contours on map (\(x\)) = 10 mm
  • Aim: Calculate the slope of the ground between the contours.

Core Concepts:

  • Contour Interval (CI): The constant vertical distance between two adjacent contours.
  • Horizontal Equivalent (HE): The actual horizontal ground distance between two adjacent contours.
  • Scale Factor: Relates map distance to ground distance: \(HE = x \times \text{Scale}\)
  • Slope Formula: \(Slope = \dfrac{CI}{HE} \times 100\%\)

Solution Method:

First, convert the map distance to actual ground distance using the scale. Then, ensure both vertical (CI) and horizontal (HE) dimensions are in the same units (meters) before calculating the percentage slope.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Horizontal Equivalent (HE):
    Map distance \(x = 10\) mm, Scale = 1:1000.
    \[HE = 10 \text{ mm} \times 1000 = 10000 \text{ mm}\]

  2. Unit Conversion:
    \[HE = 10000 \text{ mm} = 10 \text{ m}\]

  3. Calculate Slope:
    \(CI = 1\) m
    \[Slope = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 100\% = 10\%\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 10% | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 1 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A bird is resting on a point P at a height of 8 m above the Mean Sea Level (MSL). Upon hearing a loud noise, the bird flies parallel to the ground surface and reaches a point Q which is located at a height of 3 m above MSL. The ground surface has a falling gradient of 1 in 2. Ignoring the effects of curvature and refraction, the horizontal distance (in meters) between points P and Q is ___________ (in integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Leveling & Gradients

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Bird's start elevation at P = 8 m above MSL
    • Bird's end elevation at Q = 3 m above MSL
    • Ground has a falling gradient of 1 in 2
    • Bird flies parallel to the ground surface
  • Aim: Horizontal distance between P and Q in integer meters.

Core Concepts:

Gradient Definition: A gradient of "1 in \(n\)" means a vertical drop of 1 unit for every \(n\) horizontal units.\[\text{Gradient} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta H}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Vertical Drop (\(\Delta V\)):\[\Delta V = 8 \text{ m} - 3 \text{ m} = 5 \text{ m}\]

  2. Apply Gradient to find Horizontal Distance (\(\Delta H\)):
    Since the bird flies parallel to the ground with a gradient of 1 in 2:\[\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta H} \implies \Delta H = 2 \times \Delta V = 2 \times 5 = 10 \text{ m}\]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 10 m | Accepted key range: 10 to 10

Scale of vertical photograph: \(\dfrac{1}{S} = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\), where \(H - h\) is the flying height above terrain (same units as \(f\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  3. Solve for \(f\):

  4. Convert to mm: \(0.15 \times 1000 = 150\text{ mm}\)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: To finalize the direction of a survey, four surveyors set up a theodolite at a station P and performed all the temporary adjustments. From the station P, each of the surveyors observed the bearing to a tower located at station Q with the same instrument without shifting it. The bearings observed by the surveyors are 30° 30' 00'', 30° 29' 40'', 30° 30' 20'' and 30° 31' 20''. Assuming that each measurement is taken with equal precision, the most probable value of the bearing is
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Theodolite Surveying (Bearings and Most Probable Value)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four bearings of equal precision: 30° 30' 00'', 30° 29' 40'', 30° 30' 20'', 30° 31' 20''.
  • Aim: Determine the most probable value of the bearing.

Core Concepts:

When repeated measurements of equal precision are made, the most probable value is the arithmetic mean (principle of least squares for equal weights).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Express each bearing in total arc-seconds past 30° 00' 00'':
    • 30° 30' 00'' → \(30 \times 60 + 0 = 1800''\)
    • 30° 29' 40'' → \(29 \times 60 + 40 = 1780''\)
    • 30° 30' 20'' → \(30 \times 60 + 20 = 1820''\)
    • 30° 31' 20'' → \(31 \times 60 + 20 = 1880''\)
  2. Sum \(= 1800 + 1780 + 1820 + 1880 = 7280''\)
  3. Arithmetic mean \(= 7280 / 4 = 1820''\)
  4. Convert back: \(1820'' = 30' \, 20''\) → Most probable bearing = 30° 30' 20''

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 30° 30' 20'' | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A child walks on a level surface from point P to point Q at a bearing of 30°, from point Q to point R at a bearing of 90° and then directly returns to the starting point P at a bearing of 240°. The straight-line paths PQ and QR are 4 m each. Assuming that all bearings are measured from the magnetic north in degrees, the straight-line path length RP (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Traversing & Bearings

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    P to Q: Bearing \(\theta_{PQ} = 30^\circ\), Length = 4 m
    Q to R: Bearing \(\theta_{QR} = 90^\circ\), Length = 4 m
    R to P: Bearing \(\theta_{RP} = 240^\circ\)
  • Aim: Find straight-line path length RP.

Core Concepts:

Latitudes and Departures: Coordinates in surveying are defined relative to the North (\(+Y\) axis).

  • Latitude: \(\Delta Y = L\cos\theta\)
  • Departure: \(\Delta X = L\sin\theta\)

Solution Method:

Set P as the origin (0, 0). Calculate coordinates of Q, then R. Use the distance formula between P and R. The given back bearing of \(240^\circ\) serves as a consistency check.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Coordinates of Q:
    \[X_Q = 0 + 4\sin(30^\circ) = 4 \times 0.5 = 2.0\text{ m} \]\[Y_Q = 0 + 4\cos(30^\circ) = 4 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3.464\text{ m} \]
  2. Coordinates of R:
    \[X_R = 2.0 + 4\sin(90^\circ) = 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0\text{ m} \]\[Y_R = 3.464 + 4\cos(90^\circ) = 3.464 + 0 = 3.464\text{ m} \]
  3. Calculate Distance RP:
    \[RP = \sqrt{(6.0)^2 + (3.464)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 12} = \sqrt{48} = 6.928\text{ m} \]
  4. Validation via Back Bearing:
    Bearing of R from P: \(\tan^{-1}(6.0/3.464) = 60^\circ\). Back-bearing from R to P: \(60^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ\). ✓ Matches given data.
  5. Rounding to nearest integer: \(6.928 \rightarrow 7\)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 7 m | Accepted key range: [7 to 7]

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: The direct and reversed zenith angles observed by a theodolite are \( 56^\circ 00' 00'' \) and \( 303^\circ 00' 00'' \), respectively. What is the vertical collimation correction?
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Theodolite – Vertical Collimation Correction

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Direct (Face Left) zenith angle: \(Z_1 = 56^\circ\,00'\,00''\)
    • Reversed (Face Right) zenith angle: \(Z_2 = 303^\circ\,00'\,00''\)
  • Aim: Calculate the vertical collimation correction.

Core Concepts:

For a perfect instrument, zenith angles from Face Left and Face Right satisfy:\[Z_1 + Z_2 = 360^\circ \]Any deviation indicates a collimation error. The true zenith angle is:\[Z_{\text{correct}} = \dfrac{Z_1 + (360^\circ - Z_2)}{2} \]The correction applied to the direct reading is half the total error.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Check expected sum:\[Z_1 + Z_2 = 56^\circ + 303^\circ = 359^\circ \neq 360^\circ \]
  2. Total error:\[\text{Error} = 360^\circ - 359^\circ = +1^\circ\,00'\,00'' \]
  3. True zenith angle:\[Z_{\text{correct}} = \dfrac{56^\circ + (360^\circ - 303^\circ)}{2} = \dfrac{56^\circ + 57^\circ}{2} = \dfrac{113^\circ}{2} = 56^\circ\,30' \]
  4. Vertical collimation correction:\[\text{Correction} = Z_{\text{correct}} - Z_1 = 56^\circ\,30' - 56^\circ\,00' = +0^\circ\,30'\,00'' \]

Final Answer:

Vertical collimation correction \(= +0^\circ\,30'\,00''\) | Correct Option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A student is scanning his 10 inch × 10 inch certificate at 600 dots per inch (dpi) to convert it to raster. What is the percentage reduction in number of pixels if the same certificate is scanned at 300 dpi?
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Remote Sensing & GIS – Raster Data Resolution

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Certificate size: \(10\text{ inch} \times 10\text{ inch}\)
    • Case 1: Scan resolution \(R_1 = 600\text{ dpi}\)
    • Case 2: Scan resolution \(R_2 = 300\text{ dpi}\)
  • Aim: Calculate percentage reduction in number of pixels.

Core Concepts:

Total pixel count:\[N = (L \times R) \times (W \times R) = L \times W \times R^2 \]Since dimensions are fixed, \(N \propto R^2\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Pixels at 600 dpi:\[N_{600} = (10 \times 600) \times (10 \times 600) = 6000 \times 6000 = 36 \times 10^6\text{ pixels} \]
  2. Pixels at 300 dpi:\[N_{300} = (10 \times 300) \times (10 \times 300) = 3000 \times 3000 = 9 \times 10^6\text{ pixels} \]
  3. Percentage reduction:\[\%\text{ Reduction} = \dfrac{N_{600} - N_{300}}{N_{600}} \times 100 = \dfrac{36 - 9}{36} \times 100 = \dfrac{27}{36} \times 100 = 75\% \]

Quick method: Since \(N \propto R^2\), halving the resolution reduces pixels to \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\) of original → reduction \(= 75\%\). ✓

Final Answer:

75% reduction | Correct Option: (C)

Trigonometric levelling was carried out from two stations P and Q to find the reduced level (R. L.) of the top of hillock, as shown in the table. The distance between Stations P and Q is 55 m. Assume Stations P and Q, and the hillock are in the same vertical plane. The R. L. of the top of the hillock (in m) is ________________ (round off to three decimal places).

P18° 45'2.340 m100.000 m
Q12° 45'1.660 m
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Trigonometric Levelling – Inaccessible Hillock

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Distance \(PQ = 55\text{ m}\); RL of BM \(= 100.000\text{ m}\)
    • Station P: \(\alpha_P = 18^\circ 45'\), staff reading \(= 2.340\text{ m}\)
    • Station Q: \(\alpha_Q = 12^\circ 45'\), staff reading \(= 1.660\text{ m}\)
    • Since \(\alpha_P > \alpha_Q\), Station P is closer to the hillock.
  • Aim: RL of the top of the hillock.

Core Concepts:

Trigonometric Levelling:\[RL_{\text{Top}} = HI + D\tan(\alpha) \]where \(HI = RL_{BM} + \text{staff reading}\) and \(D\) = horizontal distance from station to hillock.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Heights of Instruments:\[HI_P = 100.000 + 2.340 = 102.340\text{ m} \]\[HI_Q = 100.000 + 1.660 = 101.660\text{ m} \]
  2. Convert angles:\[\alpha_P = 18^\circ 45' = 18.75^\circ, \quad \alpha_Q = 12^\circ 45' = 12.75^\circ \]\[\tan(18.75^\circ) \approx 0.339454, \quad \tan(12.75^\circ) \approx 0.226283 \]
  3. Formulate equations (let \(D\) = horizontal distance from P to hillock):
    From P: \(RL_{\text{Top}} = 102.340 + D\tan(18.75^\circ)\)
    From Q: \(RL_{\text{Top}} = 101.660 + (D+55)\tan(12.75^\circ)\)
  4. Equate and solve for \(D\):\[102.340 + 0.339454D = 101.660 + 0.226283(D+55) \]\[102.340 + 0.339454D = 101.660 + 0.226283D + 12.4456 \]\[(0.339454 - 0.226283)D = 101.660 + 12.4456 - 102.340 \]\[0.113171D = 11.7656 \Rightarrow D \approx 103.963\text{ m} \]
  5. Calculate RL of top (using P equation):\[RL_{\text{Top}} = 102.340 + 103.963 \times 0.339454 = 102.340 + 35.291 = 137.631\text{ m} \]
  6. Verification (using Q equation):\[RL_{\text{Top}} = 101.660 + (103.963+55) \times 0.226283 = 101.660 + 35.971 = 137.631\text{ m} \checkmark \]

Final Answer:

\(RL_{\text{Top}} = 137.631\text{ m}\) | Accepted range: 137.500 to 137.730

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q24

questions.question: The magnetic bearing of the sun for a location at noon is \( 183^\circ \ 30' \). If the sun is exactly on the geographic meridian at noon, the magnetic declination of the location is ________.
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Compass Surveying — Magnetic Declination

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Magnetic bearing of sun at noon: \(183°30'\)
    • Sun is exactly on the geographic meridian at noon.
  • Aim: Find magnetic declination.

2. Core Concepts:

TermDefinition
True MeridianNorth–South line through geographic poles
Magnetic MeridianDirection indicated by magnetic compass needle
True Bearing (TB)Angle from True North (clockwise)
Magnetic Bearing (MB)Angle from Magnetic North (clockwise)
Magnetic Declination (\(\delta\))Angle between True and Magnetic meridian

Fundamental Relationship:\[\text{True Bearing} = \text{Magnetic Bearing} \pm \text{Declination}\]

  • Easterly Declination (E): Magnetic North is East of True North → \(TB = MB + \delta\)
  • Westerly Declination (W): Magnetic North is West of True North → \(TB = MB - \delta\)

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

StepCalculationResult

2Magnetic Bearing given\(MB = 183°30'\)

4. Final Answer:

questions.question: If the size of the ground area is 6 km × 3 km and the corresponding photo size in the aerial photograph is 30 cm × 15 cm, then the scale of the photograph is 1 : _________________ (in integer).

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
A delivery agent is at a location R. To deliver the order, she is instructed to travel to location P along straight-line paths of RC, CA, AB and BP of 5 km each. The direction of each path is given in the table below as whole circle bearings. Assume that the latitude (L) and departure (D) of R is (0, 0) km. What is the latitude and departure of P (in km, rounded off to one decimal place)?

PathsRCCAABBP
Directions (in degrees)120090240
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Traverse Surveying

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Starting Coordinates of R: \(L_R = 0.0\text{ km},\ D_R = 0.0\text{ km}\)
    • Length of each path (\(l\)): \(5\text{ km}\)
    • Whole Circle Bearings (WCB, \(\theta\)): RC = \(120^\circ\), CA = \(0^\circ\), AB = \(90^\circ\), BP = \(240^\circ\)
  • Aim: Calculate the final Latitude (\(L\)) and Departure (\(D\)) of point P.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Latitude (\(L\)): The orthographic projection of a survey line on the North–South axis.\[L = l\cos\theta\](Positive towards North, Negative towards South)
  • Departure (\(D\)): The orthographic projection of a survey line on the East–West axis.\[D = l\sin\theta\](Positive towards East, Negative towards West)
  • Principle of Superposition:\[L_P = L_R + \sum L \quad;\quad D_P = D_R + \sum D\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the individual latitude and departure for each of the four segments (RC, CA, AB, BP).
  2. Algebraically sum the latitudes and departures.
  3. Add sums to the initial coordinates of R to get coordinates of P.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Latitude and Departure for each leg

LineBearing (\(\theta\))Latitude \(= 5\cos\theta\) (km)Departure \(= 5\sin\theta\) (km)
RC\(120^\circ\)\(5 \times (-0.5) = -2.5\)\(5 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = +4.330\)
CA\(0^\circ\)\(5 \times 1 = +5.0\)\(5 \times 0 = 0.0\)
AB\(90^\circ\)\(5 \times 0 = 0.0\)\(5 \times 1 = +5.0\)
BP\(240^\circ\)\(5 \times (-0.5) = -2.5\)\(5 \times \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -4.330\)

Step 2: Sum the Latitudes and Departures

\[\sum L = -2.5 + 5.0 + 0.0 - 2.5 = 0.0\text{ km}\]\[\sum D = +4.330 + 0.0 + 5.0 - 4.330 = +5.0\text{ km}\]

Step 3: Calculate Final Coordinates

\[L_P = L_R + \sum L = 0.0 + 0.0 = 0.0\text{ km}\]\[D_P = D_R + \sum D = 0.0 + 5.0 = +5.0\text{ km}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q23

questions.question: An aerial photograph is taken from a flight at a height of 3.5 km above mean sea level, using a camera of focal length 152 mm. If the average ground elevation is 460 m above mean sea level, then the scale of the photograph is
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Aerial Photogrammetry

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Height of flight above MSL: \(H = 3.5\) km \(= 3500\) m
    • Focal length: \(f = 152\) mm
    • Average ground elevation above MSL: \(h = 460\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the scale of the photograph.

Core Concepts:

Scale of Vertical Photograph: Ratio of the photo distance to the ground distance.

\[S = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\]

Where:

  • \(S\) = Scale (representative fraction, e.g., \(1/N\))
  • \(f\) = Focal length
  • \(H\) = Flying height above datum (MSL)
  • \(h\) = Average ground elevation above datum
  • \((H - h)\) = Flying height above average ground level

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit Conversion:
    • \(H = 3500\) m
    • \(h = 460\) m
    • \(f = 152\) mm \(= 0.152\) m
  2. Calculate Flying Height Above Ground:\[H_{ground} = H - h = 3500 - 460 = 3040 \text{ m}\]
  3. Calculate Scale:\[S = \dfrac{f}{H_{ground}} = \dfrac{0.152 \text{ m}}{3040 \text{ m}} = \dfrac{152 \text{ mm}}{3040000 \text{ mm}}\]Dividing both numerator and denominator by 152:\[S = \dfrac{1}{20000}\]The scale is \(1 : 20000\).

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{S = 1 : 20000}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.question:
A line between stations P and Q laid on a slope of 1 in 5 was measured as 350 m using a 50 m tape. The tape is known to be short by 0.1 m.

The corrected horizontal length (in m) of the line PQ will be
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Tape Corrections & Slope Corrections

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Measured Length \(L' = 350\) m, Nominal Tape Length \(l = 50\) m, Tape short by \(= 0.1\) m, Slope \(= 1\) in \(5\)
  • Aim: Find the corrected horizontal length of line PQ.

Core Concepts:

Two corrections are required:

  1. Tape Length Correction — When actual tape length differs from nominal.
  2. Slope Correction — Converting slope distance to horizontal distance.
Correction TypeFormula
Tape Correction\(L_{corrected} = L' \times \dfrac{l_{actual}}{l_{nominal}}\)
Slope Correction\(D_{horizontal} = L_{corrected} \times \cos\theta\)
Slope Ratio\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{n}\) where \(n = 5\)

Common Pitfalls:

  • Applying slope correction before tape correction (order matters).
  • Using \(\sin\theta\) instead of \(\cos\theta\) for horizontal distance.
  • Incorrect interpretation of "1 in 5" slope.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Actual Tape Length:\[l_{actual} = 50 - 0.1 = 49.9 \text{ m}\]
  2. Apply Tape Length Correction:\[L_{corrected} = 350 \times \dfrac{49.9}{50} = 350 \times 0.998 = 349.30 \text{ m}\]
  3. Calculate Slope Angle:\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2 \implies \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.2) = 11.31^\circ\]
  4. Apply Slope Correction for Horizontal Distance:\[D_{horizontal} = L_{corrected} \times \cos\theta = 349.30 \times \cos(11.31^\circ)\]\[D_{horizontal} = 349.30 \times 0.9806 = 342.52 \text{ m}\]

Sanity Check: ✓ Horizontal distance (342.52 m) < Slope distance (349.30 m) — Physically consistent.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{342.52 \text{ m}}\] Correct Option: (A)

Whole Circle Bearing (Azimuth): Measured clockwise from north (0° to 360°).

Reduced Bearing (Quadrantal Bearing): Measured from north or south toward east or west (0° to 90°).

Conversion Rules:

questions.question: If the magnetic bearing of the Sun at a place at noon is S 2° E, the magnetic declination (in degrees) at that place is
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Compass Surveying

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Magnetic Bearing of the Sun at noon = S 2° E
  • Aim: Determine the magnetic declination at the place.

3. Core Concepts:

True Bearing of the Sun at Noon: At local noon, the Sun is exactly on the True Meridian. In the Northern Hemisphere, the True Bearing of the Sun = 180° (True South).

Magnetic Declination (\(\delta\)): Angle between True North and Magnetic North.

  • Magnetic North east of True North → East declination (\(+\))
  • Magnetic North west of True North → West declination (\(-\))

Relationship: \(TB = MB + \delta_{East}\) or \(TB = MB - \delta_{West}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine True Bearing of the Sun.
  2. Convert Magnetic Bearing from Quadrantal to Whole Circle Bearing (WCB).
  3. Compare TB and MB to find declination.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. True Bearing of the Sun:
    At noon in the Northern Hemisphere: \(TB_{Sun} = 180^\circ\)
  2. Convert MB to WCB:
    S 2° E → measured from South towards East:
    \[MB_{Sun} = 180^\circ - 2^\circ = 178^\circ \]
  3. Calculate Declination:
    \[TB = MB + \delta_{East} \implies 180^\circ = 178^\circ + \delta_{East} \implies \delta_{East} = 2^\circ \]
    Physical interpretation: Magnetic North is deflected 2° east of True North. Compass reads S 2° E for True South → declination is 2° East.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2° East | Correct Option: (A)

  • Aim: Find the Fore bearing of line RS in degrees.

3. Core Concepts:

Sum of Internal Angles: For a polygon with \(n\) sides: \((2n-4) \times 90^\circ\). For \(n=4\): \(360^\circ\).
Sanity check: \(92^\circ + 68^\circ + 123^\circ + 77^\circ = 360^\circ\) ✓

Back Bearing: \(\text{BB} = \text{FB} \pm 180^\circ\)

Traverse Direction Ambiguity: The problem does not specify clockwise or counter-clockwise direction, leading to two valid geometric interpretations.

  • Case 1 (Counter-Clockwise): \(\text{FB of Next Line} = \text{BB of Previous Line} + \text{Internal Angle}\)
  • Case 2 (Clockwise): \(\text{FB of Next Line} = \text{BB of Previous Line} - \text{Internal Angle}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Case 1: Counter-Clockwise Traverse

  1. \(\text{FB}_{PQ} = 27^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{PQ} = 27^\circ + 180^\circ = 207^\circ\)
  2. \(\text{FB}_{QR} = 207^\circ + 68^\circ = 275^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{QR} = 275^\circ - 180^\circ = 95^\circ\)
  3. \(\text{FB}_{RS} = 95^\circ + 123^\circ = \mathbf{218^\circ}\)

Closure verification: \(\text{BB}_{RS} = 38^\circ \Rightarrow \text{FB}_{SP} = 115^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{SP} = 295^\circ \Rightarrow \text{FB}_{PQ} = 295^\circ + 92^\circ = 387^\circ - 360^\circ = 27^\circ\) ✓


Case 2: Clockwise Traverse

  1. \(\text{FB}_{PQ} = 27^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{PQ} = 207^\circ\)
  2. \(\text{FB}_{QR} = 207^\circ - 68^\circ = 139^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{QR} = 139^\circ + 180^\circ = 319^\circ\)
  3. \(\text{FB}_{RS} = 319^\circ - 123^\circ = \mathbf{196^\circ}\)

Closure verification: \(\text{BB}_{RS} = 16^\circ \Rightarrow \text{FB}_{SP} = 16^\circ - 77^\circ + 360^\circ = 299^\circ \Rightarrow \text{BB}_{SP} = 119^\circ \Rightarrow \text{FB}_{PQ} = 119^\circ - 92^\circ = 27^\circ\) ✓

Both traverse layouts are physically and mathematically valid. Either 196° or 218° is a correct answer depending on the assumed direction of the traverse.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 196° or 218°  |  Accepted key range: 196 to 196 OR 218 to 218

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:

3. Core Concepts:

Closing Error Vector: In a closed traverse, if the end point does not perfectly coincide with the start point, the gap is the closing error. Its Cartesian components are the sum of latitudes (\(\sum L\)) and sum of departures (\(\sum D\)).

Magnitude (Length):\[e = \sqrt{(\sum L)^2 + (\sum D)^2} \]

Direction (Bearing):\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{|\sum D|}{|\sum L|} \]

Quadrant Determination:

  • Latitude (\(+\)) \(\rightarrow\) North
  • Departure (\(-\)) \(\rightarrow\) West
  • Resulting Quadrant \(\rightarrow\) North-West (NW)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the magnitude using the Pythagorean theorem.
  2. Compute the angle using the inverse tangent function.
  3. Convert the decimal degree angle to degrees, minutes, and seconds (DMS).
  4. Determine the quadrant from the signs of \(\sum L\) and \(\sum D\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Length (\(e\)):\[e = \sqrt{(2.1)^2 + (-2.8)^2} = \sqrt{4.41 + 7.84} = \sqrt{12.25} = 3.50\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Bearing Angle (\(\theta\)):\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.8}{2.1}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) = 53.1301^\circ \]
  3. Convert to DMS format:
    \(0.1301^\circ \times 60' = 7.806'\)
    \(0.806' \times 60'' \approx 48''\)
    \(\therefore\; \theta = 53^\circ\, 7'\, 48''\)
  4. Determine the quadrant:
    \(\sum L\) is positive (N) and \(\sum D\) is negative (W) \(\Rightarrow\) NW
    Therefore, Bearing is \(53^\circ\, 7'\, 48''\text{ NW}\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.50 m and 53°7'48" NW | Correct option: (A)

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Angle of depression from instrument at P to vane at Q: \(\theta = 45^\circ\)
    • Height of vane above station Q: \(h_{vane} = 2\text{ m}\)
    • Horizontal distance PQ: \(D = 20\text{ m}\)
    • RL of Benchmark (BM): \(433.050\text{ m}\)
    • Backsight (BS) reading on staff at BM: \(2.905\text{ m}\)
    • Curvature and refraction errors neglected.
  • Aim: Determine the Reduced Level (RL) of station Q.

3. Core Concepts:

Height of Instrument (HI): Established by taking a backsight reading on a known benchmark: \[\text{HI} = \text{RL of BM} + \text{BS} \]

Trigonometric Leveling: The vertical drop (\(V\)) from the instrument line of sight to the target: \[V = D \tan(\theta) \]

RL of Target Station: \[\text{RL}_Q = \text{HI} - V - h_{vane} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the HI at station P.
  2. Calculate the vertical distance \(V\) from the instrument axis down to the vane using the depression angle.
  3. Subtract \(V\) from HI to get the RL of the vane.
  4. Subtract the height of the vane to find the RL of station Q (ground level).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Height of Instrument (HI)

\[\text{HI} = 433.050 + 2.905 = 435.955\text{ m} \]

Step 2: Calculate Vertical Drop (\(V\))

\[V = D \tan(\theta) = 20 \times \tan(45^\circ) = 20 \times 1 = 20\text{ m} \]

Step 3: Calculate RL of the Vane

\[\text{RL}_{\text{vane}} = \text{HI} - V = 435.955 - 20 = 415.955\text{ m} \]

Step 4: Calculate RL of Station Q

\[\text{RL}_Q = \text{RL}_{\text{vane}} - h_{vane} = 415.955 - 2 = 413.955\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 413.955 m | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q55

questions.question: A theodolite is set up at station A. The RL of instrument axis is 212.250 m. The angle of elevation to the top of a 4 m long staff, held vertical at station B, is 7°. The horizontal distance between stations A and B is 400 m. Neglecting the errors due to curvature of earth and refraction, the RL (in m, round off to three decimal places) of station B is _________.
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Trigonometric Levelling)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Setup Station: A
    • RL of Instrument Axis: \(212.250\text{ m}\)
    • Target Station: B; Staff length = \(4.000\text{ m}\) (sighted at top, so \(h = 4.000\text{ m}\))
    • Angle of elevation to staff top, \(\alpha = 7^\circ\)
    • Horizontal distance, \(D = 400\text{ m}\)
    • Curvature and refraction neglected.
  • Aim: Determine the Reduced Level (RL) of the ground at station B in metres, rounded to three decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Trigonometric Levelling:

  • Vertical height difference: \(V = D\tan(\alpha)\)
  • RL of targeted point \(=\) RL of Instrument Axis \(+ V\) (angle of elevation)
  • RL of ground at B \(=\) RL of targeted point \(- h\)

Combined equation: \[RL_B = RL_{\text{Inst. Axis}} + V - h \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate vertical height difference \(V\) using trigonometry.
  2. Add \(V\) to RL of instrument axis to get RL of the staff top at B.
  3. Subtract staff length \(h\) to get ground RL at B.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Compute Vertical Distance (\(V\))

\[V = D\tan(\alpha) = 400 \times \tan(7^\circ) = 400 \times 0.12278 = 49.114\text{ m} \]

Step 2: Compute RL of Station B

\[RL_B = 212.250 + 49.114 - 4.000 \] \[RL_B = 261.364 - 4.000 = 257.364\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 257.364 m | Accepted key range: 257.200 to 257.600

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A survey line was measured to be 285.5 m with a tape having a nominal length of 30 m. On checking, the true length of the tape was found to be 0.05 m too short. If the line lay on a slope of 1 in 10, the reduced length (horizontal length) of the line for plotting of survey work would be
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Linear Measurements)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Measured length \((L_m) = 285.5\text{ m}\)
    • Nominal tape length \((l_n) = 30\text{ m}\)
    • Tape error \(= 0.05\text{ m}\) too short \(\implies\) True tape length \((l_t) = 30 - 0.05 = 29.95\text{ m}\)
    • Slope \(= 1\text{ in }10\)
  • Aim: Determine the reduced horizontal length of the line.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Tape Correction: If a tape is too short, the measured distance is longer than the actual distance.\[\text{True Slope Length }(L_t) = L_m \times \left( \dfrac{l_t}{l_n} \right) \]
  • Slope Correction: To plot survey work, horizontal distance \((H)\) must be found.\[H = L_t \times \cos\theta \]Note: A slope of 1 in 10 in standard topography conventionally means \(\tan\theta = 1/10\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Apply the correction for absolute length to find the true length along the slope.
  2. Determine \(\cos\theta\) from the given slope gradient.
  3. Multiply the true slope length by \(\cos\theta\) to obtain the horizontal projection.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Apply Tape Correction

\[L_t = 285.5 \times \left( \dfrac{29.95}{30} \right) = 285.5 \times 0.998333 = 285.024\text{ m} \]

Step 2: Slope Correction

Slope gradient is \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{10}\).

\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{10^2 + 1^2}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{101}} \approx 0.995037 \]

Even if interpreting 1 in 10 as \(\sin\theta = 1/10\), \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - 0.1^2} \approx 0.99498\), which yields an identical final rounded answer.

Step 3: Horizontal Reduced Length

\[H = L_t \times \cos\theta = 285.024 \times 0.995037 = 283.609\text{ m} \approx 283.6\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Horizontal Length \(= 283.6\) m | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A staff is placed on a benchmark (BM) of reduced level (RL) 100.000 m and a theodolite is placed at a horizontal distance of 50 m from the BM to measure the vertical angles. The measured vertical angles from the horizontal at the staff readings of 0.400 m and 2.400 m are found to be the same. Taking the height of the instrument as 1.400 m, the RL (in m) of the theodolite station is ________
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Trigonometric Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Reduced Level (RL) of Benchmark (BM) \(= 100.000\) m
    • Horizontal distance to staff, \(D = 50\) m
    • Staff readings: \(h_1 = 0.400\) m and \(h_2 = 2.400\) m
    • Measured vertical angles to these readings are equal in magnitude.
    • Height of theodolite instrument (HI) \(= 1.400\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the RL of the theodolite station.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Trigonometric Levelling: In a theodolite, vertical angles are measured from the horizontal line of sight (line of collimation).
  • If the vertical angles to two different staff readings are identical in magnitude, one must be an angle of elevation (\(+\theta\)) and the other an angle of depression (\(-\theta\)).
  • Because the distances from the horizontal crosshair to the two staff readings are \(+D\tan\theta\) and \(-D\tan\theta\) respectively, the horizontal line of sight will hit exactly at the midpoint of these two staff readings.
  • \(\text{Central staff reading} = \dfrac{h_1 + h_2}{2}\)
  • \(\text{RL of Line of Collimation} = \text{RL of BM} + \text{Central Staff Reading}\)
  • \(\text{RL of Station} = \text{RL of Line of Collimation} - \text{Height of Instrument}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Find the exact point where the horizontal line of sight hits the levelling staff.
  2. Determine the RL of the Line of Collimation.
  3. Subtract the theodolite's height to find the ground elevation of the station.

Note: The 50 m horizontal distance is superfluous data meant to distract; it cancels out geometrically.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find horizontal reading:\[h_{\text{center}} = \dfrac{0.400 + 2.400}{2} = 1.400\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate RL of the Line of Collimation (staff is placed on the BM):\[\text{RL of Collimation} = 100.000\text{ m} + 1.400\text{ m} = 101.400\text{ m} \]
  3. Calculate RL of Theodolite Station:\[\text{RL of Station} = \text{RL of Collimation} - \text{HI} = 101.400\text{ m} - 1.400\text{ m} = 100.000\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

RL of Station \(= 100.000\) m | Accepted key range: 100 to 100

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
The data from a closed traverse survey PQRS (run in the clockwise direction) are given in the table
LineIncluded angle (in degrees)
PQ88
QR92
RS94
SP89

The closing error for the traverse PQRS (in degrees) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Traversing

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Closed traverse PQRS (4 sides, \(n = 4\))
    • Direction: Clockwise
    • Included angles: PQ = 88°, QR = 92°, RS = 94°, SP = 89°
  • Aim: Compute the closing angular error in degrees.

3. Core Concepts:

Geometric Sanity Check: In surveying, for a closed polygon of \(n\) sides:

  • Sum of interior angles \(= (2n - 4) \times 90°\)
  • Sum of exterior angles \(= (2n + 4) \times 90°\)

For a 4-sided traverse, interior angles sum to \(360°\). Exterior angles sum to \(1080°\).

Error Calculation: Closing Error = Measured Sum − Theoretical Sum.

4. Solution Method:

Sanity Check: Though textbooks define the "included angle" in a clockwise traverse as the exterior angle, the measured values are roughly \(\sim 90°\). It is physically impossible for the exterior angles of a quadrilateral to sum anywhere near \(360°\) (they must sum to \(1080°\)). Therefore, the surveyor recorded the interior angles.

  1. Calculate the sum of the provided included (interior) angles.
  2. Determine the theoretical sum for a 4-sided closed traverse.
  3. Find the absolute magnitude of the closing error.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Sum of Measured Angles (\(\Sigma_{measured}\)):\[\Sigma_{measured} = 88° + 92° + 94° + 89° = 363° \]
  2. Theoretical Sum (\(\Sigma_{theoretical}\)):\[\Sigma_{theoretical} = (2(4) - 4) \times 90° = 4 \times 90° = 360° \]
  3. Closing Error Calculation:\[\text{Error} = \Sigma_{measured} - \Sigma_{theoretical} = 363° - 360° = +3° \]The magnitude of the closing error is \(3°\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3 | Accepted key range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q33

questions.question: A camera with a focal length of 20 cm fitted in an aircraft is used for taking vertical aerial photographs of a terrain. The average elevation of the terrain is 1200 m above mean sea level (MSL). What is the height above MSL at which an aircraft must fly in order to get the aerial photographs at a scale of 1:8000?
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Photogrammetry

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Focal length of camera, \(f = 20\) cm
    • Average elevation of terrain, \(h = 1200\) m above MSL
    • Scale of photograph, \(S = 1:8000\)
  • Aim: Determine the flying height of the aircraft above Mean Sea Level (\(H\)).

3. Core Concepts:

Scale of a Vertical Aerial Photograph: The scale is the ratio of the focal length of the camera to the flying height of the aircraft above the terrain.

\[S = \dfrac{f}{H - h} \]

Unit Discipline: Ensure \(f\), \(H\), and \(h\) are all in the same units (meters) before calculation.

4. Solution Method & Execution:

  1. Step 1: Unit Conversion
    \(f = 20\text{ cm} = 0.2\text{ m}\), \(S = \dfrac{1}{8000}\)
  2. Step 2: Substitute into the scale formula and solve for \(H\).\[\dfrac{1}{8000} = \dfrac{0.2}{H - 1200} \]\[H - 1200 = 8000 \times 0.2 = 1600 \]\[H = 1600 + 1200 = 2800 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2800 m | Correct option: (B)

questions.explanation:

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: 4-leg closed traverse with Northing/Southing (Latitudes) and Easting/Westing (Departures).
  • Aim: Determine the length and direction (WCB) of closure.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Latitude (\(\Delta N\) / \(\Sigma L\)): Northing is Positive (+), Southing is Negative (−).
  • Departure (\(\Delta E\) / \(\Sigma D\)): Easting is Positive (+), Westing is Negative (−).
  • The Error of Closure vector (\(e\)) describes how much the traverse misses the origin.
  • The Correction / Closing Line vector is exactly equal and opposite to the error.

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Sum the Latitudes (\(\Sigma L\))\[\Sigma L = \text{Northings} - \text{Southings} \]\[\Sigma L = (101 + 419) - (437 + 83) = 520 - 520 = 0 \text{ m} \]
  2. Step 2: Sum the Departures (\(\Sigma D\))\[\Sigma D = \text{Eastings} - \text{Westings} \]\[\Sigma D = (173 + 558) - (96 + 634) = 731 - 730 = +1 \text{ m (Easting)} \]
  3. Step 3: Determine Length of Closure\[\text{Length} = \sqrt{(\Sigma L)^2 + (\Sigma D)^2} = \sqrt{0^2 + 1^2} = 1 \text{ m} \]

questions.question: A square area (on the surface of the earth) with side 100 m and uniform height, appears as 1 cm² on a vertical aerial photograph. The topographic map shows that a contour of 650 m passes through the area. If focal length of the camera lens is 150 mm, the height from which the aerial photograph was taken, is
questions.explanation:
Geomatics | Photogrammetry

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area of square on ground: \(100 \text{ m} \times 100 \text{ m} = 10{,}000 \text{ m}^2\)
    • Area on aerial photograph: \(1 \text{ cm}^2\)
    • Elevation of terrain: \(h = 650 \text{ m}\)
    • Camera focal length: \(f = 150 \text{ mm} = 0.15 \text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Height from which the photograph was taken (\(H\)) above Mean Sea Level.

2. Core Concepts:

Linear Scale (\(S\)): Ratio of distance on the map to distance on the ground.

\[S = \dfrac{f}{H - h} \]

Areal Scale (\(S^2\)): Square of the linear scale.

\[S^2 = \dfrac{\text{Area on Photograph}}{\text{Area on Ground}} \]

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Determine the Areal Scale
    Convert photograph area to SI units:\[A_{photo} = 1 \text{ cm}^2 = 1 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2 \]\[A_{ground} = 10{,}000 \text{ m}^2 = 10^4 \text{ m}^2 \]\[S^2 = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-4}}{10^4} = 10^{-8} \]
  2. Step 2: Determine the Linear Scale (\(S\))\[S = \sqrt{10^{-8}} = 10^{-4} = \dfrac{1}{10{,}000} \]
  3. Step 3: Calculate the Flying Height (\(H\))
    Using \(S = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\):\[\dfrac{1}{10{,}000} = \dfrac{0.15}{H - 650} \]\[H - 650 = 0.15 \times 10{,}000 = 1500 \]\[H = 1500 + 650 = 2150 \text{ m} \]

4. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2150 m | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q36

questions.question: A level instrument at a height of 1.320 m has been placed at a station having a Reduced Level (RL) of 112.565 m. The instrument reads -2.835 m on a levelling staff held at the bottom of a bridge deck. The RL (in m) of the bottom of the bridge deck is
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Reduced Level (RL) of station: \(112.565\text{ m}\)
    • Height of instrument setup: \(1.320\text{ m}\)
    • Levelling staff reading (inverted, at bottom of bridge deck): \(-2.835\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the RL of the bottom of the bridge deck.

3. Core Concepts:

Height of Instrument (HI) Method:\[HI = RL_{\text{station}} + \text{Setup Height}\]

Inverted Staff Convention: When a point is above the line of sight (e.g., a ceiling or soffit of a deck), the staff is held inverted. The reading is treated as negative algebraically.\[RL_{\text{point}} = HI - \text{Staff Reading}\]

4. Solution Method:

First, calculate the elevation of the line of sight (HI). Then, subtract the negative staff reading to obtain the elevation of the bridge deck. Subtracting a negative inherently adds it, reflecting that the point physically sits above the line of sight.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Height of Instrument (HI):\[HI = 112.565\text{ m} + 1.320\text{ m} = 113.885\text{ m}\]
  2. Calculate RL of Bridge Deck:\[RL_{\text{deck}} = HI - (\text{Staff Reading})\]\[RL_{\text{deck}} = 113.885 - (-2.835)\]\[RL_{\text{deck}} = 113.885 + 2.835 = 116.720\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 116.720 m | Correct option: (A)

questions.question: An aerial photograph of a terrain having an average elevation of 1400 m is taken at a scale of 1:7500. The focal length of the camera is 15 cm. The altitude of the flight above mean sea level (in m, up to one decimal place) is ______

questions.explanation:

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis & Evaluation
  • Given Data: Observed Fore Bearings (FB) and Back Bearings (BB) for a traverse.
  • Aim: Identify which station(s) are most likely affected by local attraction.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Local Attraction: A magnetic anomaly at a station that uniformly deflects the magnetic needle.
  • Detection: If \(|\text{FB} - \text{BB}| = 180^\circ 00'\) for a line, both end stations of that line are considered free from local attraction.
  • Consistency Principle: The error caused by local attraction at any specific station must be a constant value for all bearings observed from that station.

4. Solution Method & Error Detection:

Evaluate the FB–BB differences for all lines:

  • Line PQ: FB \(= 46^\circ 15'\), BB \(= 226^\circ 15'\) \(\implies |226^\circ 15' - 46^\circ 15'| = 180^\circ 00'\) — Stations P and Q appear free from local attraction.
  • Line ST: FB \(= 321^\circ 45'\), BB \(= 141^\circ 45'\) \(\implies |321^\circ 45' - 141^\circ 45'| = 180^\circ 00'\) — Stations S and T appear free from local attraction.

Checking for physical consistency at Station R:

  1. Via Q (free station):
    • Correct FB of QR = Observed FB \(= 108^\circ 15'\)
    • Correct BB of QR \(= 108^\circ 15' + 180^\circ = 288^\circ 15'\)
    • Observed BB of QR (from R) \(= 286^\circ 15'\)
    • Local attraction error at R \(= 286^\circ 15' - 288^\circ 15' = -2^\circ 00'\)
  2. Via S (free station):
    • Correct BB of RS (from S) = Observed BB \(= 20^\circ 30'\)
    • Correct FB of RS (from R) \(= 20^\circ 30' + 180^\circ = 200^\circ 30'\)
    • Observed FB of RS \(= 201^\circ 30'\)
    • Local attraction error at R \(= 201^\circ 30' - 200^\circ 30' = +1^\circ 00'\)

The required correction at Station R is \(-2^\circ\) via line QR, but \(+1^\circ\) via line RS. Since local attraction represents a single magnetic deviation at a fixed location, the error must be uniform for all readings taken from that station. The data is therefore physically inconsistent — no single set of local attractions can produce these readings. GATE authorities recognized this critical flaw and awarded Marks to All for this question.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Data is physically inconsistent (error at R evaluates to both \(-2^\circ\) and \(+1^\circ\)).  |  Correct option: Marks to All

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 2 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
Two towers, A and B, standing vertically on a horizontal ground, appear in a vertical aerial photograph as shown in the figure.


The length of the image of the tower A on the photograph is 1.5 cm and of the tower B is 2.0 cm. The distance of the top of the tower A (as shown by the arrowhead) is 4.0 cm and the distance of the top of the tower B is 6.0 cm, as measured from the principal point p of the photograph. If the height of the tower B is 80 m, the height (in meters) of the tower A is ___________
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Photogrammetry (Relief Displacement)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Relief displacement of tower A: \(d_A = 1.5 \text{ cm}\)
    • Relief displacement of tower B: \(d_B = 2.0 \text{ cm}\)
    • Radial distance to top of tower A from principal point: \(r_A = 4.0 \text{ cm}\)
    • Radial distance to top of tower B from principal point: \(r_B = 6.0 \text{ cm}\)
    • Height of tower B: \(h_B = 80 \text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Find the height of tower A, \(h_A\) (in meters).

3. Core Concepts:

Relief Displacement (\(d\)): In a vertical aerial photograph, a vertical object standing above the datum appears to lean outwards from the principal point. The length of its image on the photograph is its relief displacement.

Formula:\[d = \dfrac{r \cdot h}{H} \]where \(d\) = relief displacement, \(r\) = radial distance from the principal point to the top of the object, \(h\) = height of the object, \(H\) = flying height of the aircraft above the base of the object.

Both towers are on the same horizontal ground, hence the flying height \(H\) is identical for both.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use the data for Tower B to determine the flying height \(H\).
  2. Use the computed flying height \(H\) and the data for Tower A to determine the height \(h_A\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate flying height \(H\) using Tower B
    Rearranging the relief displacement formula: \(H = \dfrac{r_B \cdot h_B}{d_B}\)\[H = \dfrac{6.0 \text{ cm} \times 80 \text{ m}}{2.0 \text{ cm}} = \dfrac{480}{2.0} = 240 \text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate height of Tower A (\(h_A\))
    Rearranging for \(h_A\): \(h_A = \dfrac{d_A \cdot H}{r_A}\)\[h_A = \dfrac{1.5 \text{ cm} \times 240 \text{ m}}{4.0 \text{ cm}} = \dfrac{360}{4.0} = 90 \text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 90 m | Accepted key range: 89 to 91

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 2 | CE Q55

questions.question: An observer standing on the deck of a ship just sees the top of a lighthouse. The top of the lighthouse is 40 m above the sea level and the height of the observer’s eye is 5 m above the sea level. The distance (in km, up to one decimal place) of the observer from the lighthouse is ___________
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Levelling (Curvature and Refraction)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Height of lighthouse: \(H = 40 \text{ m}\)
    • Height of observer's eye: \(h = 5 \text{ m}\)
    • Observer just sees the top of the lighthouse (line of sight is tangent to the Earth's curved surface).
  • Aim: Find the total distance separating the observer and the lighthouse in km (up to 1 decimal place).

3. Core Concepts:

Combined Curvature and Refraction: Earth's curvature lowers objects from the horizontal line of sight, while atmospheric refraction lifts them slightly.

Visible Horizon Distance Formula: Distance \(d\) (in km) to the visible horizon for an object of height \(h\) (in meters):\[d = 3.855\sqrt{h} \]

Inter-visibility: Total distance when two elevated points just see each other:\[D = d_1 + d_2 = 3.855\sqrt{H} + 3.855\sqrt{h} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute the visible distance to the observer's horizon (\(d_1\)).
  2. Compute the visible distance to the lighthouse's horizon (\(d_2\)).
  3. Add both distances.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Observer's Horizon Distance (\(d_1\)):\[d_1 = 3.8553\sqrt{5} = 3.8553 \times 2.236 = 8.620 \text{ km} \]
  2. Lighthouse's Horizon Distance (\(d_2\)):\[d_2 = 3.8553\sqrt{40} = 3.8553 \times 6.3245 = 24.383 \text{ km} \]
  3. Total Distance (\(D\)):\[D = 8.620 + 24.383 = 33.003 \approx 33.0 \text{ km} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 33.0 km | Accepted key range: 32.5 to 33.5

questions.question: The vertical angles subtended by the top of a tower T at two instrument stations set up at P and Q, are shown in the figure. Readings taken from these two stations on a leveling staff placed at the benchmark (BM = 450.000 m) are also shown in the figure. The reduced level of the top of the tower T (expressed in m) is _______________
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Trigonometric Leveling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Benchmark RL: \(450.000\text{ m}\)
    • Distance between instruments P and Q: \(60\text{ m}\)
    • Angle of elevation from P to tower top: \(10.5^\circ\)
    • Angle of elevation from Q to tower top: \(16.5^\circ\)
    • Staff reading at P: \(0.555\text{ m}\); Staff reading at Q: \(2.555\text{ m}\) (from diagram)
  • Aim: Determine the Reduced Level (RL) of the top of the tower T.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Height of Instrument: \(HI = \text{BM RL} + \text{Staff Reading}\)
  • Elevation of tower top from each station: \(RL_T = HI + D\tan(\theta)\), where \(D\) is horizontal distance from instrument to tower.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Height of Instruments:\[HI_Q = 450.000 + 2.555 = 452.555\text{ m} \]\[HI_P = 450.000 + 0.555 = 450.555\text{ m} \]
  2. Formulate Distance Equations:
    Let horizontal distance from Q to tower \(= x\). Distance from P to tower \(= x + 60\).\[RL_T = 452.555 + x\tan(16.5^\circ) \quad \cdots (1) \]\[RL_T = 450.555 + (x+60)\tan(10.5^\circ) \quad \cdots (2) \]
  3. Solve for \(x\):
    Using \(\tan(16.5^\circ) = 0.29621\) and \(\tan(10.5^\circ) = 0.18534\):\[452.555 + 0.29621x = 450.555 + 0.18534x + 60(0.18534) \]\[2.000 + 0.29621x = 0.18534x + 11.1203 \]\[0.11087x = 9.1203 \implies x = 82.261\text{ m} \]
  4. Calculate \(RL_T\):\[RL_T = 452.555 + 82.261 \times 0.29621 = 452.555 + 24.366 = 476.921\text{ m} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 476.92 m | Accepted key range: [476.5, 477.5]

questions.question: A circular curve of radius R connects two straights with a deflection angle of 60°. The tangent length is

4. Solution Method & Execution:

questions.title: GATE CE 2016 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A tall tower was photographed from an elevation of 700 m above the datum. The radial distances of the top and bottom of the tower from the principal points are 112.50 mm and 82.40 mm, respectively. If the bottom of the tower is at an elevation 250 m above the datum, then the height (expressed in m) of the tower is _________
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Photogrammetry

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Flying altitude above datum: \(H = 700\text{ m}\)
    • Ground elevation of tower bottom above datum: \(h_b = 250\text{ m}\)
    • Image radial distance to tower top: \(r_t = 112.50\text{ mm}\)
    • Image radial distance to tower bottom: \(r_b = 82.40\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Determine the physical height of the tower (\(h_{\text{tower}}\)) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Relief Displacement: The radial outward shift of an object's top on an aerial photograph relative to its bottom due to its elevation above the datum.\[d = r_t - r_b \]
  • Tower Height Formula (from similar triangles in aerial camera projection):\[h_{\text{tower}} = \dfrac{d \cdot (H - h_b)}{r_t} \]where \((H - h_b)\) is the relative flying height above the tower base.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Subtract radial distances to find relief displacement (\(d\)).
  2. Calculate the effective flying altitude relative to the tower base (\(H - h_b\)).
  3. Use the relief displacement formula to solve for \(h_{\text{tower}}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Relief Displacement (\(d\)):\[d = 112.50 - 82.40 = 30.10\text{ mm} \]
  2. Effective Flying Height:\[H - h_b = 700 - 250 = 450\text{ m} \]
  3. Tower Height:\[h_{\text{tower}} = \dfrac{30.10 \times 450}{112.50} = \dfrac{13545}{112.50} = 120.4\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 120.4 m | Accepted key range: 120 to 121

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 1 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: In a closed loop traverse of 1 km total length, the closing errors in departure and latitude are 0.3 m and 0.4 m, respectively. The relative precision of this traverse will be:
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Traverse Surveying

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Total loop traverse perimeter: \(L = 1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}\)
    • Closing error in departure: \(e_D = 0.3\text{ m}\)
    • Closing error in latitude: \(e_L = 0.4\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Determine the relative precision.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Total Closing Error (\(e\)): \[e = \sqrt{e_D^2 + e_L^2} \]
  • Relative Precision: \[\text{Relative Precision} = \frac{e}{L} = \frac{1}{L/e} \] expressed in \(1:N\) format.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate total linear closing error using Pythagoras.
  2. Normalize to \(1:N\) format.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total linear closing error:
    \[e = \sqrt{(0.3)^2 + (0.4)^2} = \sqrt{0.09 + 0.16} = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5\text{ m} \]
  2. Relative precision:
    \[\frac{e}{L} = \frac{0.5}{1000} = \frac{1}{2000} \]
  3. Standard format:
    \[\text{Relative Precision} = 1:2000 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1 : 2000  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 1 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: In a survey work, three independent angles X, Y and Z were observed with weights \(W_X, W_Y, W_Z\), respectively. The weight of the sum of angles X, Y and Z is given by:
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Theory of Errors

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Independent angles \(X, Y, Z\) with weights \(W_X, W_Y, W_Z\).
  • Aim: Determine the weight of their sum \((X + Y + Z)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Error Propagation for independent quantities: Variance of a sum equals the sum of individual variances: \[\sigma_S^2 = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_Z^2 \]
  • Weight-Variance relationship: \(W \propto \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2} \implies \sigma^2 \propto \dfrac{1}{W}\)

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the inverse weight relationship into the variance equation:

\[\frac{1}{W_S} = \frac{1}{W_X} + \frac{1}{W_Y} + \frac{1}{W_Z} \]

Taking the reciprocal:

\[W_S = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{W_X} + \dfrac{1}{W_Y} + \dfrac{1}{W_Z}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 1 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: In a region with magnetic declination of 2°E, the magnetic Fore bearing (FB) of a line AB was measured as N79°50'E. There was local attraction at A. To determine the correct magnetic bearing of the line, a point O was selected at which there was no local attraction. The magnetic FB of line AO and OA were observed to be S52°40'E and N50°20'W, respectively. What is the true FB of line AB?
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Compass Surveying & Local Attraction

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Declination = \(2^\circ\text{ E}\)
    • Measured Magnetic FB of \(AB\) = \(N\,79^\circ 50'\,E\)
    • Local attraction exists at \(A\); Point \(O\) is free from local attraction
    • Measured Magnetic FB of \(AO\) = \(S\,52^\circ 40'\,E\)
    • Measured Magnetic FB of \(OA\) = \(N\,50^\circ 20'\,W\)
  • Aim: Determine the True Fore Bearing (FB) of line \(AB\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • The station free from local attraction yields correct bearings.
  • Back Bearing (BB) = Fore Bearing (FB) \(\pm 180^\circ\) (or reversed quadrants: N \(\leftrightarrow\) S, E \(\leftrightarrow\) W).
  • Correction at station = Correct Bearing − Observed Bearing.
  • True Bearing = Corrected Magnetic Bearing + Declination (East is positive).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Since \(O\) is free from local attraction, the measured FB of \(OA\) is correct.
  2. Deduce the correct BB of \(OA\), which is the correct FB of \(AO\).
  3. Compare correct FB of \(AO\) with the observed FB of \(AO\) at \(A\) to find the local attraction correction.
  4. Apply correction to the observed FB of \(AB\) to get the corrected magnetic bearing of \(AB\).
  5. Apply magnetic declination to find True Bearing.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Correct Bearings based on station O:
    Observed (correct) FB of \(OA = N\,50^\circ 20'\,W\)
    Correct FB of \(AO\) (BB of \(OA\)) = \(S\,50^\circ 20'\,E\)
  2. Calculate correction at A (using WCB):
    • Correct FB of \(AO\) in WCB \(= 180^\circ - 50^\circ 20' = 129^\circ 40'\)
    • Observed FB of \(AO\) in WCB \(= 180^\circ - 52^\circ 40' = 127^\circ 20'\)
    • Correction at \(A = 129^\circ 40' - 127^\circ 20' = +2^\circ 20'\)
  3. Correct Magnetic Bearing of AB:
    Observed FB of \(AB\) in WCB \(= 79^\circ 50'\)
    \[\text{Corrected Mag. FB of } AB = 79^\circ 50' + 2^\circ 20' = 82^\circ 10' \quad (N\,82^\circ 10'\,E) \]
  4. Convert to True Bearing:
    \[\text{True FB of } AB = 82^\circ 10' + 2^\circ 00' = 84^\circ 10' \quad (N\,84^\circ 10'\,E) \]

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q34

questions.question: In a leveling work, sum of the Back Sight (B.S.) and Fore Sight (F.S.) have been found to be 3.085 m and 5.645 m respectively. If the Reduced Level (R.L.) of the starting station is 100.000 m, the R.L. (in m) of the last station is _____________.

    • Reduced Level of First Station, \(\text{R.L.}_{\text{first}} = 100.000\) m
